verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse_text.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

reading: You are waiting for your exam results this Friday and finding you cannot eat. Krishna tells Arjuna, your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits, so do not let the outcome stop you. When the result day arrives, let your focus rest on what you have already done, not on the number that appears.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna stands between two armies and feels he cannot fight. Krishna tells him that a person has a right only to the work itself, never to its fruits. The work must be done fully. The outcome must not be owned. One should not let the fear of what comes next stop the action. Your exam results are coming out on Friday and the wait has taken away your appetite. The verse points to the work you have already done, not the mark you will see.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on the five causes behind every action.
verse_text.line: Every result has five causes: the setting, the doer, the tools, the efforts, and the unseen. You're one of them.
verse_text.translation: The seat, the doer, the various instruments, the many kinds of effort, and fifth, providence: these are the five causes of every action.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that every result has five causes: the setting, the doer, the tools, the efforts, and the unseen. You are only one of them. Your Friday result sits inside a web far larger than your own doing, so the weight of the outcome does not rest solely on you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: No sincere effort here is ever wasted. Even a little of it shields you from great fear.
verse_text.translation: On this path no effort is lost and no harm results. Even a little of this practice protects one from great fear.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that no sincere effort is ever wasted here, and even a little of it shields you from great fear. With your exam results arriving on Friday, your honest studying already stands as real ground beneath you, regardless of what the mark sheet holds. Let that steadiness be the concrete thing you return to when Friday comes.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna reminds Arjuna of his duty as a warrior and what retreat would cost him.
verse_text.line: Hold pleasure and pain, gain and loss, win and defeat as equal. Then step in and act.
verse_text.translation: Treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike, then engage in the fight. Done this way, you will incur no wrong.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to treat pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat as equal, then step into action. Since your exam results arrive on Friday and your appetite has vanished, this steadiness gives you ground to stand on right now. You can step toward the result without your worth riding on whether you win or lose.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Yoga is skill in action: doing the work well, without being bound by it.
verse_text.translation: One joined to this understanding casts off both good and bad results here. So devote yourself to yoga; yoga is skill in action.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that yoga is skill in action: doing the work well without being bound by it. Since your exam results arrive on Friday and you cannot eat, you could try bringing your full attention to one small task today, letting the outcome fall where it may.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna, who asks why he must act at all if understanding is higher.
verse_text.line: Do the work that's yours. Doing something beats doing nothing; even living needs action.
verse_text.translation: Do your allotted work, for action is better than inaction. Even the maintenance of your body would not be possible without action.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to do his allotted work, because action is better than inaction, and even the body cannot survive without it. With your exam results coming out on Friday and the stress making you unable to eat, you could try taking one small, concrete step today—like reviewing one page or organizing your notes—rather than freezing. This keeps your body and mind moving, just as Krishna says action sustains life itself.

story.title: Jambavan reminds Hanuman who he is
story.summary: At the edge of the ocean, the search party looking for Sita stopped. One by one, each warrior said how far he could leap, and none could reach Lanka. Hanuman sat quietly at the back. The old bear-king Jambavan turned to him and reminded him who he was: his birth, his strength, everything he had already done. Why are you holding back? Hanuman stood, grew to his full size, and made ready to leap.
story.lesson: Sometimes you need someone to remind you what you are capable of.

days.reading: At the edge of the ocean, the search party stopped, and each warrior named a limit until none could reach Lanka. Jambavan turned to Hanuman sitting quietly at the back and reminded him of his birth, his strength, and all he had already done, asking why he held back. Like the result waiting on Friday, your ability is already there; let someone else’s reminder help you step forward into what you can do.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna, seeing his own family in the enemy ranks, collapses in grief before the battle.
verse_text.line: Shaking limbs, a dry mouth, a racing body: the Gita opens with a panic attack, not a hero.
verse_text.translation: My limbs give way, my mouth is parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.

reading: Your limbs shake and your mouth goes dry. Arjuna tells Krishna that his body trembles and his hair stands on end right before battle. Like him, your body is reacting to sudden loss and uncertainty. Let this trembling be seen as simply a signal that safety has shifted, not as a flaw in you.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He sees his own kin standing in the enemy ranks. His body collapses under the weight of what he must do. He tells Krishna that his limbs give way, his mouth is parched, his body trembles and his hair stands on end. The verse proposes that even a capable warrior can freeze when the ground beneath him shifts. It names the physical reality of fear before any teaching begins. Your body is echoing that same sudden shift. The savings cover three months, yet the ground still feels unsteady.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You lied to your wife about money and she found out. Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against his will, as if pushed by force. This verse speaks to your guilt by naming the force you felt inside, not by judging the lie itself. You can sit with that question the next time the weight returns.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against his own will, as if pushed by some force from outside. Krishna answers that it is desire. When a desire is blocked or unmet, it turns into anger. That anger clouds a person's wisdom and judgment. The verse proposes that a person can see this process clearly and then master the desire instead of being driven by it. The guilt you carry now points to a force that moved you before you chose the lie. Naming that inner push is the first step toward understanding it without letting it run you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.
verse_text.line: Even if you were the worst wrongdoer of all, the raft of wisdom would carry you across.
verse_text.translation: Even if you are the most sinful of all sinners, you will cross over all wrongdoing by the raft of knowledge alone.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that even if you were the worst wrongdoer of all, the raft of wisdom would carry you across. Guilt says you are what you did, yet this verse sees you crossing over from it while the river remains behind. You can step onto that raft now, letting the lie to your wife stay in the water you have left.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.
verse_text.line: As a blazing fire turns wood to ash, real understanding burns away the hold of past actions.
verse_text.translation: As a blazing fire reduces fuel to ashes, Arjuna, so the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that as a blazing fire turns wood to ash, real understanding burns away the hold of past actions. The lie you told your wife happened, yet the grip of replaying it and the shame can burn away. Let the fire of this understanding meet the concrete fact of what you said, until only the ash of the event remains.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on simple, wholehearted devotion.
verse_text.line: Even if you've done great wrong, the moment you turn wholeheartedly, count yourself among the good.
verse_text.translation: Even if one of very bad conduct worships me with undivided devotion, he should be regarded as good, for he has resolved rightly.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that even someone of very bad conduct who worships with undivided devotion is to be counted among the good, because their resolve is right. Your lie about money still stands, yet this turn toward honesty places you in a different company than your guilt claims. Let this resolve shape how you speak to your wife today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on simple, wholehearted devotion.
verse_text.line: Such a person soon turns good and finds lasting peace. Mark it: no one devoted to me is ever lost.
verse_text.translation: He soon becomes righteous and attains lasting peace. Kaunteya, declare it boldly: my devotee never perishes.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that someone devoted to him soon becomes righteous and finds lasting peace, and that his devotee never perishes. You could choose one small, honest action today to begin turning your conduct toward what you value. This shift starts with what you do next, not with who you were before.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna's final counsel: act with devotion, reflect, choose, and take refuge.
verse_text.line: Lean on me alone. I will free you from every wrong. Don't worry.
verse_text.translation: Abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in me alone. I will free you from all sins; do not grieve.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to abandon all duties and take refuge in him alone, promising to free him from every wrong and telling him not to grieve. After owning what you did with your wife, you could set down the weight of that lie for the rest of today. Let the truth you already faced be enough for this moment.

story.title: Yudhishthira after the war
story.summary: Yudhishthira won the war and could not bear it. So many of his own family were dead, and he blamed himself. He wanted to give up the throne and go into the forest for good. One after another, his brothers, Draupadi, and the sages Devasthana and Vyasa argued with him about duty, guilt, grief and the shortness of life. Slowly he agreed to stay and rule, and to spend what was left of his life doing good.
story.lesson: Guilt and grief are real, but they are not the end. The good you do next counts.

days.reading: Yudhishthira won the war yet wanted to disappear because so many of his own family had died and he blamed himself. This speaks to your guilt after your wife found out about the lie. The story shows that grief and blame are real, but they do not have to be the end; the good you do next counts.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: Your brother took your share of the house, and that leaves you angry. Ram says only one sorrow burns his heart: that his father did not tell him himself about Bharata's coronation. Today, that silence of not being spoken to directly may echo your own hurt, where the wrong done feels sharper because it came without warning or open word from someone close.
meaning: Rama speaks to Kaikeyi after he has accepted fourteen years of exile. He has agreed to leave without anger. Yet one thing still burns him. He tells her that the news itself is not the wound. What hurts most is that his father did not come to him and speak the truth directly. He is saying that the manner of delivery can cut deeper than the command itself. Your brother took your share of the house, and the anger you feel carries the weight of being bypassed rather than confronted.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': the poet to his own hope.
verse_text.line: I swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. Hope, how much longer will you make me dance?
verse_text.translation: I somehow put up with the taunts of the wicked while trying to please them; I held back my tears and laughed with an empty heart; I folded my hands even before people whose minds were numbed by money. Hope, futile hope, how much more will you make me dance?

reading: You are carrying the weight of having your analysis taken as someone else's. Bhartrihari tells his own hope that he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart, folding his hands before those numbed by money. Today, you can let that forced smile rest. Your analysis still belongs to you, even if it was spoken under another name.
meaning: The poet Bhartrihari speaks to his own hope from the section Censure of craving. He recounts how he endured mockery from wicked people while trying to please them. He held back his tears and laughed with an empty heart. He even folded his hands before people whose minds were numbed by money. He asks hope how much longer it will make him dance in this futile way.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You wake with the same meeting replaying in your head. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, and that holding it feels like holding the wind. Right now, your thoughts are that wind, circling the criticism you heard. Let the verse name what is happening: the mind is simply doing what it does, and the wind does not obey the archer.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the field of battle. He has just confessed his confusion and grief. Now he admits that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He says it is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna does not deny this. He agrees that the mind is difficult to master, but he adds that steady practice and letting go can train it. Your mind is replaying that meeting because it is doing exactly what Arjuna described. It is not a failure on your part.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You find yourself thinking about good food, and when someone stops you, anger rises. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born, and from attachment comes desire, which turns into anger when blocked. Today, that thought of food can quietly build before the moment someone stands in your way, leaving the anger already there when the interruption happens.
meaning: Krishna is answering Arjuna, who has asked what a steady person looks like. Krishna explains that when someone dwells on objects, attachment is born. From that attachment comes desire, and when that desire is blocked, it turns into anger. Your mind is already resting on good food before anyone steps near you. The anger you feel is not only about the interruption.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: With your son in Canada and the house quiet, Krishna tells Arjuna, See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me. You might feel far from home, yet this view says the bond between you and what you love does not break because of distance. The quiet rooms can hold that same unbroken seeing.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching him meditation and the nature of a settled mind. He tells Arjuna that when a person sees him everywhere and sees everything within him, then he is never lost to that person, and that person is never lost to him. The verse proposes that a steady gaze, returned to again and again with moderation, keeps the bond intact even when the mind wanders. Your son is far away and the rooms are still. This verse names a way of seeing that does not break across distance, and it offers the quiet house as a place where that seeing can rest.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: Feeling lonely now that you are retired, you may be searching for connection. Krishna tells Arjuna to see him in everything and everything in him, saying he never loses him, nor he him. This invites you to notice the familiar world around you as a place where you remain held, right where you are.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching him how to meditate and what a settled mind looks like. He tells Arjuna that if a person sees him in every being and sees every being within him, then Krishna is never lost to that person, and that person is never lost to Krishna. After years of work, the house feels quieter. This idea invites you to notice that you remain held by the world around you, right where you are.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna tells Arjuna where the divine is found.
verse_text.line: The divine lives in the heart of every being, yours included.
verse_text.translation: The Lord dwells in the heart of every being, Arjuna, moving all beings by his power as if mounted on a machine.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the Lord dwells in the heart of every being, moving all beings by his power. This means you carry someone constant inside you, never alone in your own chest. Let that presence be the ground beneath your feet today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna tells Arjuna who he is to every being.
verse_text.line: I am your goal, your support, your witness, your home, your shelter and your friend.
verse_text.translation: I am the goal, the sustainer, the master, the witness, the home, the refuge and the friend; the origin and the dissolution, the ground, the treasure-house and the undying seed.

days.reading: In one verse Krishna lists what he is to every being: goal, support, witness, home (nivāsaḥ), shelter (śaraṇam) and friend (suhṛt). If you've been missing all of those, this verse names them together.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, briefly describing meditation and the peace it brings.
verse_text.line: The divine is the well-wisher of every being, you included. Knowing this, you find peace.
verse_text.translation: Knowing me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great lord of all the worlds, and the friend of all beings, one attains peace.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the divine is the friend of all beings, including you, and that knowing this brings peace. After resting in the truth that the divine lives in every heart, you now have ground to stand on: this friend asks nothing in return, simply dwelling within you. Let that quiet presence be your steady companion today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Feel others' joy and pain as if they were your own. That is the highest practice.
verse_text.translation: One who, by comparison with himself, sees the same everywhere, Arjuna, whether in pleasure or in pain, is considered the highest yogi.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to feel others' joy and pain as his own, calling this the highest practice. As you sit with your loneliness today, you could try noticing the quiet feelings of a stranger or neighbor as if they were your own, letting that shared awareness settle beside you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, describing the qualities of the person dear to God.
verse_text.line: Hate no one. Be friendly and kind, free of 'mine' and ego, steady in pain and joy, and forgiving.
verse_text.translation: One who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free from possessiveness and ego, even in pain and pleasure, and forgiving,

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the one dear to God hates no one, is friendly and kind, free from possessiveness and ego, steady in pain and joy, and forgiving. After reflecting on divine presence as your home, you could offer a small kindness to someone today without claiming anything as yours. This steadiness in pleasure and pain opens a path to companionship.

story.title: Ram and Sugriva become friends
story.summary: Ram had lost his home, and his wife Sita had been taken. Sugriva, driven out by his brother, had lost his home and his wife too. They met in the forest and swore friendship before a fire. Then Sugriva brought out the jewels Sita had dropped as she was carried away. Ram broke down at the sight of them, and Sugriva, who had his own grief, comforted him: in trouble, think it through steadily, and lean on your friend.
story.lesson: Two people in trouble can carry each other.

days.reading: In the Kishkindha Kanda, Ram and Sugriva, both driven from their homes and grieving their lost wives, meet in the forest and swear friendship before a fire. Sugriva then offers Sita’s fallen jewels, and though Ram breaks down, Sugriva, bearing his own sorrow, steadies him by saying to think things through and lean on a friend. As you sit with your own loneliness, this scene shows two exiles meeting in grief and choosing to carry each other, pointing you toward the steady comfort of shared presence.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that when someone dwells on objects, attachment is born, then desire, and then anger. You are feeling angry right now. This verse suggests that your anger may have grown from dwelling on something and wanting it to be different. You might notice what you keep returning to in your mind today.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna what a person of steady mind looks like in speech, sitting and walking. Krishna answers by describing someone content within and master of the senses. He then traces how dwelling on objects breeds attachment, attachment turns into desire, and blocked desire becomes anger that leads to ruin. Your anger may have grown from returning to the same thought over and over. The verse invites you to notice what you keep dwelling on today.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: My heart feels heavy as stone, but I don't cry, because of what people would think.
verse_text.translation: Though my heart is packed tight with the stones of life's sorrows, I don't let my tears fall, only out of fear of what my own people would think.

reading: It sounds like you're carrying something very heavy right now.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: My heart feels heavy as stone, but I don't cry, because of what people would think.
verse_text.translation: Though my heart is packed tight with the stones of life's sorrows, I don't let my tears fall, only out of fear of what my own people would think.

reading: It sounds like you're carrying something very heavy right now.

verse_text.speaker: Vibhishan
verse_text.setting: Vibhishan, Ravana's good-hearted brother, describes his life in Ravana's court.
verse_text.line: I live here like the tongue among the teeth.
verse_text.translation: Son of the wind, hear how I live: like the poor tongue among the teeth. Friend, knowing me to be without support, will the Lord of the Sun dynasty ever show me grace?

reading: It sounds like home doesn't feel safe right now.

verse_text.speaker: Nidagha
verse_text.setting: Nidagha on craving, continued.
verse_text.line: Craving is a restless monkey: never in one place, never satisfied, reaching even where it cannot go.
verse_text.translation: It sets foot even where no one can go; even when satisfied it strives in vain; it never stays long in one place: craving is a restless monkey.

reading: You are looking for the best laptop under 60k for coding. Nidagha tells Ribhu that craving is a restless monkey: it never stays in one place and is never satisfied. Today, that same restlessness may be driving your search, jumping from specs to prices without landing. Notice when this monkey leaps next, and simply watch where it lands.
meaning: Nidagha speaks to his teacher Ribhu after returning from a pilgrimage feeling empty. He describes how craving behaves like a restless monkey. It moves constantly and never finds a place to rest. It reaches even into places no one can access. When it seems satisfied it still strives without result. It does not stay long in any one spot. That same restlessness may be moving through your search for a machine right now.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna says that people turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom, and all four are welcome. You carry a curious mind into your working days, and this line meets that curiosity as a genuine path. Let that openness guide where you place your attention today.
meaning: Krishna speaks this to Arjuna while they stand on the field before battle. He is explaining why some people miss the divine and who instead turns toward it. He names four kinds of good people who worship him. These are the distressed, the curious, those who seek wealth, and the wise. He makes clear that every reason is welcome. Your curiosity at work is not a distraction from the search. It is one of the four genuine ways to begin.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

days.reading: Arjuna tells Krishna he is stricken by weakness and confused about what is right, asking plainly to be taught as a student. From the verse's view, this surrender comes from not knowing the self. You stand at the start of your week with the Gita, ready to learn what it actually says about ordinary life.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that contact between the senses and their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain, which come and go and do not last, so he should bear them patiently. Since you are curious about where the Gita begins, this grounds you in what actually changes and what stays steady. Notice one sensation today that arrives and passes, and simply let it go.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse_text.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits, and not to let that make you stop. For your working days, this means the task in front of you belongs to you, while what comes after does not. Let your next project be the ground you stand on today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse_text.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to lift himself by his own self and not let himself sink, for the self alone is the friend of the self. Since you are curious about how the Gita speaks to ordinary life, you could notice one moment today when you push yourself down, and instead offer yourself the same steady support you would give a friend.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.
verse_text.line: Learn from those who have seen the truth: approach with humility, ask real questions, and serve.
verse_text.translation: Learn it by bowing down, by questioning, and by service. Those who are wise and have seen the truth will teach you that knowledge.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to learn by bowing down, asking real questions, and serving those who have seen the truth. Since you are curious about what the Gita actually says, you could approach one trusted source today with a genuine question about its teachings and listen closely to the answer.

story.title: Action with devotion: surrender
story.summary: Krishna urges Arjuna to offer all action, warns that ego will only trip him, tells him to reflect fully and then choose, and finally to take refuge in him alone and not grieve.
story.lesson: Reflect fully, choose freely, and set down the fear.

days.reading: The Lord tells Arjuna, 'Reflect on this fully, then do as you wish,' after eighteen chapters of teaching, and follows with, 'Come to me alone for refuge; I will free you from all wrongs, do not grieve.' This leaves the decision with you while offering a final refuge, speaking to your curiosity by trusting you to weigh what you have heard before choosing your path.
